faq.answer: No. Pursuit, standards, and effort are different from attainment. Skills, resources, opportunity, feedback, and the suitability of the goal still matter. Neither a success nor a failure establishes the tendency on its own.
faq.question: Does strong Achievement Striving guarantee success?

faq.answer: No. Incentives can coexist with interest, standards, and other motives. Examine the person's choices and effort in context. Behavior appearing only under one incentive should first be interpreted within that setting, rather than generalized to all goals.
faq.question: Does pursuing a bonus mean the motivation is not Achievement Striving?

faq.answer: Not necessarily. The additional demand may not serve the purpose, its cost may be too high, or the person may be pursuing a demanding aim elsewhere. Look at meaningful choices and usable opportunities instead of treating one stopping decision as a whole-person verdict.
faq.question: Is choosing a sufficient result the same as lacking ambition?

faq.answer: No. Standards, concerns about mistakes, and self-evaluation need separate examination and can overlap in different ways. The facet cannot diagnose those patterns. Ask what the standard is for and how the person responds when it is missed.
faq.question: Does a high score establish perfectionism?

faq.answer: They can be tested as ways of managing a particular activity. Check whether they help action, useful feedback, and acceptable effort. A short-term improvement does not establish a stable trait or score change.
faq.question: Can small goals or stop rules change the trait?

faq.answer: Ask which support they want and review the purpose, constraints, and stopping conditions together. Respect a decision to reduce or retire a goal. Avoid making output the sole measure of the relationship, and do not use a personality label to dismiss persistent distress.
faq.question: How can I support someone who is deeply invested in a goal?

not_for: Do not use this page for clinical diagnosis or as the sole basis for hiring or admission.
method_boundary.summary: Use this page to understand personality concepts and examine everyday behavior. Interpret actual scores using the instrument’s scoring method, reference sample, and intended use.

sections.body:
Achievement Striving concerns pursuing demanding goals, holding high standards, and investing effort toward them. It does not guarantee that the result meets the standard. Someone beginning a difficult project can show substantial pursuit while still lacking experience, access, or useful feedback.

In this site's NEO/IPIP-NEO vocabulary, Achievement Striving belongs to [Conscientiousness](/en/personality/big-five/conscientiousness). The [public IPIP item key](https://ipip.ori.org/newNEOFacetsKey.htm) covers standards and quality alongside hard work, acting on plans, and substantial investment. The facet therefore includes effort rather than only the height of a target. The [official comparison table](https://ipip.ori.org/newNEO_FacetsTable.htm) describes similar NEO and IPIP constructs, not interchangeable instruments. Other Big Five tools can use different facet structures.

This explanation does not establish that a particular assessment measured the facet. If a result reports only a domain, do not invent a facet score. Actual attainment needs separate evidence about the work and its conditions.
sections.heading: A demanding aim is not an achieved result

sections.body:
[Competence](/en/personality/big-five/facets/competence) concerns perceived capability; Achievement Striving concerns pursuit, standards, and investment. Believing you can do something is different from wanting to pursue a more demanding version. Neither belief nor desire is an objective ability test.

[Self-Discipline](/en/personality/big-five/facets/self-discipline) places more emphasis on beginning and sustaining action, including when interest fades. Its behavioral territory can overlap with Achievement Striving. The distinction is useful, but it is not a promise that one facet chooses the goal while another mechanically guarantees completion.

Competitiveness and status seeking concern comparison and position, which may or may not be part of a goal. Perfectionism can involve high standards together with concerns about mistakes or self-evaluation; it is not captured by a simple contrast between improvement and flawless work. Ask what a missed standard means to the person and what they do next. An Achievement Striving score cannot establish those answers.
sections.heading: Related ideas overlap without being identical

sections.body:
A stronger tendency may involve choosing demanding goals, maintaining high standards, and investing substantial effort toward them. A weaker tendency may involve less inclination to pursue such goals or to invest beyond what is needed to get by. These descriptions concern patterns across usable choices and opportunities. Maintaining an already demanding standard can be relevant without repeatedly raising it; choosing a sufficient outcome on one occasion does not establish a weaker tendency. Nor does one declined promotion describe every part of a life.

A stronger tendency does not guarantee sustained execution, delayed gratification, or better output. A weaker tendency does not establish better recovery, contentment, or an ability to finish more projects. A person may currently have no worthwhile opportunity, or may want a challenge that their resources cannot support.

An intermediate result can reflect moderate pursuit, differences between settings, or uncertainty in responses. It does not establish wise goal selection or ideal balance. These are positions on a continuum, not separate types or rankings of personal worth.
sections.heading: What high, low, and intermediate scores can mean

sections.body:
A goal can matter for several reasons: interest, income, recognition, competition, obligation, or avoiding a loss. Achievement Striving does not require motivation to be entirely intrinsic. Nor does working intensely under an incentive establish a broad tendency by itself.

Consider a contractor taking on extra work near the end of a billing period. The behavior may reflect a demanding personal target, a financial need, a client's pressure, or a combination. Ask how much choice exists, which standard the contractor is pursuing, and what happens across naturally different periods and activities.

If effort rises only under that particular constraint, keep the explanation specific to it. If the person also repeatedly chooses challenging, meaningful aims when similar pressure is absent, a wider provisional description may become reasonable. There is no need to withdraw income, create a penalty, or test someone's loyalty to a goal.
sections.heading: External incentives are part of the context

sections.body:
Imagine a home cook trying to develop a reliably enjoyable meal for a small gathering. They choose a more demanding recipe, repeat trials, and ask people what needs adjustment. Early versions may still be disappointing. The chosen challenge and investment are observable; the quality of the meal needs feedback of its own.

Limited equipment, ingredient cost, and available evenings affect what can be attempted. A week without another trial could mean no workable opportunity, an ordinary decision to use the time elsewhere, or a change in the goal. Those explanations cannot be collapsed into a low-striving label.

A different cook might produce excellent food from a familiar recipe without seeking a harder target at all. That result reflects something about the finished work and existing skill; it does not by itself establish strong Achievement Striving. Neither person should have effort or ambition inferred solely from the plate.
sections.heading: A concrete goal shows why effort and quality need separate evidence

sections.body:
When effort keeps expanding, ask what the additional work is for. Is it correcting a problem that matters, exploring a worthwhile improvement, or raising the requirement after the useful result is already available? Include the time, recovery, competing commitments, and demands placed on other people in that assessment.

A stop rule can define the purpose of a particular goal: meet the agreed use and quality requirements, submit the work, and leave optional extensions for another occasion. Stopping at that point is not proof of weak striving. Continuing is not proof of strong striving. Financial pressure or role requirements may also restrict the ability to stop, so the difficulty should not automatically be assigned to personality.

Persistent exhaustion or distress that interferes with everyday life deserves attention to the actual workload and, when needed, assessment by a qualified professional. A facet label cannot establish a health condition or explain away ongoing difficulty.
sections.heading: Stopping and continuing both need an explanation

sections.body:
Take one activity that matters to you and a specific hypothesis: 'When I have usable time and resources for this activity, I usually choose a demanding target and invest effort toward it.' On a naturally occurring occasion, you have those conditions and a real choice, but select a less demanding target and do only what that target requires. Keep the occasion in the record. One exception does not overturn 'usually'; repeated differences under comparable conditions may call for a narrower description. Stopping after meeting an already demanding target is not the same counterexample.

Record your own account of wanting to pursue the goal, feeling satisfied, or still wanting more separately from the action. Submitting the work or taking a break does not establish that you felt content, lacked ambition, or found stopping easy. A report of wanting more also does not establish that further effort occurred.

For the opposite hypothesis—'Under those conditions, I rarely choose a demanding target and invest effort toward it'—repeated voluntary choices and effort in that same activity are relevant contrasting evidence. Keep the activity and conditions fixed rather than substituting success elsewhere. Distinguish a usable opportunity followed by a different choice, no usable opportunity, and a record in which no contrasting example was found. An inaccessible promotion, unaffordable competition, or short observation period cannot confirm the label.
sections.heading: Let ordinary counterexamples narrow the interpretation

sections.body:
Choose a meaningful activity with limited consequences and use the hypothesis above: 'When I have usable time and resources for this activity, I usually choose a demanding target and invest effort toward it.' During ordinary occasions, note the necessary outcome, your chosen standard, external demands, actual choice, usable time and resources, investment, and your own account of what you wanted or felt. Record feedback and the result separately from the pursuit.

Include opportunities followed by choosing a demanding target and investing effort, usable opportunities without that combination, and occasions with no usable opportunity. Meeting an already demanding standard still counts as pursuing it; an optional extension is only one possible clue. Repeated, voluntary pursuit under reasonably comparable conditions can support retaining a local description. A pattern restricted to a particular activity or incentive calls for a narrower interpretation. If overload, imposed work, or inaccessible resources dominate the record, suspend the trait conclusion. Not finding a contrasting occasion is not confirmation. This is practical observation, not a short-term personality validation.

For a separate deliberate trial, define a sufficient result, one optional stretch, an effort limit, and a stopping point. Check whether the extra demand produces an identifiable benefit and whether its cost remains acceptable. Reduce or remove it if the cost outweighs the benefit; retain the method if it serves the goal. If a reminder, tracking routine, or goal no longer helps, adjust or stop using it. Keep useful support in place; there is no need to withdraw it to make a test. Mark the trial as an intervention rather than ordinary behavior. Its effect does not establish a stable personality change.

For trouble getting started, read [Self-Discipline](/en/personality/big-five/facets/self-discipline). For doubts about capability, read [Competence](/en/personality/big-five/facets/competence). If a personal target displaces existing promises, see [Dutifulness](/en/personality/big-five/facets/dutifulness). The [Conscientiousness guide](/en/personality/big-five/conscientiousness) and [30-facet guide](/en/personality/big-five/facets) explain the wider framework.
sections.heading: Observe first, then try one bounded goal

seo.description: Understand Achievement Striving, its high and low tendencies, and how it differs from self-discipline. Separate goals and effort from success and assess their costs.
seo.title: Achievement Striving in the Big Five: High and Low Explained

personality_public_content_asset_v1.summary: Achievement Striving describes pursuing demanding goals with high standards and effort. It does not guarantee success or require endlessly raising the bar.
